schools.summary: Calvin measures the trial — a promised land that will not feed them, God trying the fathers so that we might not be effeminate and cowardly under temptation — and identifies this Abimelech as a descendant, the name being a royal title meaning 'My father the king'; Gill places the famine in Canaan with the Targum of Jonathan.

Henry reads the famine as providence testing what the word had taught, and finds the doctrine in three famines compared — Jacob sent down to Egypt, Isaac forbidden, Abraham left to his liberty — since God proportions his people's trials to their strength.

Clarke lays out the chapter's argument by sections, cannot date the famine beyond its falling after Abraham's death, and leaves open whether this Abimelech and Phichol are the men of the earlier narrative or their descendants.

Keil and Delitzsch frame the chapter as a life resembling Abraham's yet drawn to fit Isaac's own character, and read the halt at Gerar as a command not to leave the land promised to him; Ellicott places Isaac at the well Lahai-Roi, too far south for Gerar to lie on his direct road into Egypt.

debates.question: Is this the Abimelech of Abraham’s day?

sides.position: a descendant; Abimelech was a royal title among the Gerarites as Pharaoh was in Egypt
it cannot be determined — both men may still have been living if they were young in Abraham’s time

2.pericope_label: The Lord appears: sojourn in this land

schools.summary: Calvin takes the prohibition as God sparing a weaker son, since he assists our infirmities and will not suffer his own to be tempted beyond what they are able to bear, and denies that Abraham's obedience was the reason the promise was ratified; Gill keeps the command plain, that Isaac was to stay within Canaan, Gerar being part of it.

Clarke grounds the prohibition in character rather than in any stated reason, holding that while a man acknowledges God in all his ways God will direct his steps without giving him the reasons of his providence; Wesley draws the practical edge, that only those have the benefit of God's covenant with their parents who tread the steps of their obedience.

Ellicott counts the appearings — only twice in Isaac's life, and sixty years since the last revelation — and contrasts that rarity with the ordinary Providence under which most of the patriarchs' days were spent; Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the sister told of at Gerar.

debates.question: Why was Isaac forbidden the Egypt his father had been allowed?

sides.position: because there was more infirmity in the son, and God anticipates the evils that might ensnare his people
because of a wide difference in firmness and decision of character, the reason never being told to Isaac himself

schools.summary: Calvin makes the imitation of Abraham the aggravation rather than the excuse, and lays two charges — an evasion not far removed from a lie, and the exposing of his wife by absolving her from conjugal fidelity; Gill reads the townsmen's inquiry as arising from the prevalence of lust, though restrained, adultery being detestable to them where fornication was made no account of.

Henry draws two lessons — that very good men have sometimes been guilty of very great faults, and that we are apt to imitate the weaknesses of those we value — and says the falls of those gone before us are rocks on which others have split, recorded like buoys set to save future mariners.

Clarke asks whether Abraham ever told his son of the same fault, turns aside to advise parents on confessing former failings, and settles that the words were a lie, Rebekah being only Isaac's cousin; Wesley repeats Henry almost word for word on the dissimulation.

Ellicott marks how differently this episode ran from Abraham's: the people rather than the king make the inquiry, no annoyance follows the denial, and there are no presents, no marks of respect and no friendship, peace coming only after long quarrels.

debates.question: Were Isaac’s words an outright lie?

sides.position: yes — Abraham could speak literally of Sarah, but Rebekah was only Isaac’s cousin, and a lie is any word spoken with intent to deceive
he did not in express terms deny his wife, but resorted to an evasion not far removed from a lie

outliers.note: Turns the verse into counsel for parents — whether and how to tell children of one's own former failings, with the warning that the advice itself may serve as an incentive to the evil.

themes: the men of the place asked him

8.pericope_label: Abimelech looks out at a window

schools.summary: Calvin finds the mercy in the manner of the rescue, a heathen king stirred up to correct the fault mildly instead of the wife being torn away as twice befell Sarah, and infers from Abimelech's judgment both Isaac's purity and his own age's decline in chastity; Gill takes the long stay from the idiom that days were prolonged to him, days being sometimes put for years.

Clarke will not define the word for sporting beyond its evident force, thinks Abimelech may have had some knowledge of God's designs for Abraham's family, and notes that death was adultery's punishment among Canaanites, Philistines and Hebrews alike; Wesley repeats that Abimelech is a royal title.

Ellicott counts eighty years since Abraham's sojourn and doubts the same king can be reigning, yet allows that king and people keep the good character previously deserved, the Philistines being at this period a feeble colony of strangers restrained by a sense of their own weakness.

themes: thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us

schools.summary: Calvin answers how a man commanded to live as a stranger could sow at all — in a hired field, since buying land would have been contrary to his vocation and Moses would not have passed over so notable an offence — and ascribes the whole increase to God's blessing rather than to Isaac's industry; Gill sets the sowing after the settlement with Abimelech.

Henry marks the year above all: while others scarcely reaped at all Isaac reaped a hundredfold in a famine, and he adds an observation for the encouragement of poor tenants who occupy other people's lands and are honest and industrious.

Clarke reads the hundredfold as literally a hundredfold of barley with the Septuagint, perhaps a rare crop in Gerar, though the words may be taken generally for a very great increase as in the parable of the sower; Wesley presses the same emphasis on the time.

Ellicott sees a stage of life changing, Isaac at first doing no more than the Bedaween who sow a plot, wait for the crop and then resume their roving, and cites Herodotus on Babylonian yields against our Lord's hundredfold as the extreme of productiveness in Palestine.

debates.question: How could Isaac sow, having been commanded to live as a stranger?

sides.position: he had bought a field, the word being read as a possession
he sowed in a hired field; purchase was contrary to his vocation, and a tent is mentioned immediately after

themes: a stranger with no land of his own

13.pericope_label: Envy, the stopped wells, and the sending away

schools.summary: Calvin draws the rule that earthly blessings are never pure and perfect but mixed with troubles, lest quiet and indulgence render us negligent, and calls the stopping of a father's wells the extreme of cruelty; Gill counts the wealth in sheep, oxen, asses and camels, and admires Isaac's departing at once, taking neither to argument nor to arms.

Clarke hears the greatness in a Hebrew root repeated three times, makes the dismissal the first recorded instance of ostracism with Bacon's saying attached, and doubts the rendering that would make Isaac mightier than the king of whole tribes.

Ellicott presses the word behind 'great store of servants', which literally means making employment and answers to our word business, and explains the narrow defile in whose bed water can generally be found by digging; Keil and Delitzsch fix the retreat in the undulating land of Gerar.

outliers.note: Reads the expulsion as the earliest recorded ostracism and would re-translate the king's words: 'thou hast obtained much wealth among us, and my people are envious of thee.'

themes: go from us, for thou art mightier

schools.summary: Calvin measures the straits before praising the patience — Isaac had four hundred armed domestics after his father's example and used none of them — and reads behind the stopped wells the ancient practice of interdicting an enemy from fire and water; Gill sets the first quarrel on the border and has Isaac remove further off to cut off all pretence.

Henry finds in the names Contention and Hatred the nature of worldly things, that they are make-bates and occasions of strife, and the lot of the most peaceable, who avoid striving and yet cannot avoid being striven with.

Clarke prefers Houbigant's reading 'the servants of Abraham', renders the spring a well of living waters and an emblem of the Spirit's influences, and calls Isaac the most implicit follower on record of the command Resist not evil; Wesley glosses Esek and Rehoboth and draws the moral that those who study to be quiet seldom fail of being so.
Keil and Delitzsch look on to Beersheba, where Abraham had spent long, and where the promises would be renewed by night.

23.pericope_label: Beersheba: the appearing and the altar

schools.summary: Calvin weighs the oracle against the well and finds one word of God heavier than the accumulated mass of all good things, explains what a vision was for and why Satan's counterfeits cannot deceive those whose eyes God illuminates, and takes the altar for public worship built for a whole household; Gill has Isaac return once the famine was over, to the grove his father had planted.

Clarke reads the appearing as comfort exactly timed, Isaac having returned to the place where his noble father had lately died with the memory of his wrongs and his loss upon him; Wesley draws the plain comfort that those may remove with confidence who are sure of God's presence wherever they go.
Keil and Delitzsch look on from the night appearing to the treaty that follows it.

themes: the Lord appeared the same night
fear not, for I am with thee

schools.summary: Calvin reads the king's approach as evidence of a secret divine impulse — why else humble himself to supplicate a private man rather than send for him and command him? — and concludes that the minds of men are in the hand of God; Gill supposes Abimelech feared Isaac would resent his expulsion and turn his riches and power against him.

Henry makes it a rule that settling friendships needs the wisdom of the serpent as well as the innocence of the dove, while granting that the visit came at all because when a man's ways please the Lord he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.

Clarke thinks a royal title and a name of office likelier than the survival of Abraham's two men, and reports the Targum's 'company' and the Septuagint's Ochozath the paranymph against taking Ahuzzath for a proper name.

Ellicott sets the visit in the politics of Canaan — the Philistines an alien race who feared a Semitic alliance, and Abraham's old confederacies with Amorites and Hittites — and says Isaac's return forced the king to choose between peace and war.

sides.position: no — with the Targum it means a company, an escort of friends who came with the king
uncertain, but if a name the rendering should be "Ahuzzath his friend", his confidential adviser and privy counsellor

28.pericope_label: We saw certainly that the Lord was with thee

schools.summary: Calvin makes their confession a testimony that God is the author of all good things, wonders that they should still fear an inoffensive man — they judge his probity by their own conduct — and turns Isaac's forbearance into a rule that those who have estranged themselves are not to be repelled when they offer themselves again; Gill spells out what the Philistines had seen, the blessing following Isaac even after he left them.

Clarke has them propose a covenant binding both parties and ratified in the most solemn manner; Wesley reads 'thou art the blessed of the Lord' as persuasion to overlook the injuries offered, since those whom God blesses can afford to forgive, their worst enemy being unable to do them real hurt.

debates.question: Is "thou art now the blessed of the Lord" mere flattery?

sides.position: commonly so explained, as men flatter when they ask a favour
holders: the common reading, reported by Calvin

sides.position: no — it is an argument that no grief need remain, God having treated Isaac so exactly according to his own wish

themes: let there be an oath betwixt us
that thou wilt do us no hurt
we have done unto thee nothing but good

30.pericope_label: The oath and the well Shebah

schools.summary: Calvin makes the swearing the legitimate use of God's name, granted because dissimulation and inconstancy make men distrustful of each other, and argues that the well kept the name Abraham gave it, the Hebrew word being ambiguous enough to carry both covenants at once; Gill prefers 'oath' to Jerome's 'fulness' and explains why the morning was the fitter time for so solemn a transaction.

Clarke supposes the feast was made on the sacrifice offered at the covenant, credits early rising with the health and longevity of the primitive world, and finds the old name restored with an added letter that extends it from an oath to satisfaction and abundance.
Ellicott leaves open which of the two wells at Beersheba this was, and takes the phrase 'unto this day' for a note added by Ezra and the men of the Great Synagogue after the return from Babylon.

debates.question: What does the name Shebah mean here?

sides.position: fulness, from the abundance of water in the well
an oath, from the oath just sworn, the two circumstances having met on one day

schools.summary: Calvin reads the marriages as a kind of prelude of Esau's rejection, and ascribes the harshness of the daughters-in-law to the wonderful counsel of God, lest the parents grow by degrees favourable to a reprobate people; on the two wives he notes only that polygamy had so far prevailed that the vicious custom had acquired the force of law. Gill observes that Esau married at the age his father had.

Henry locates the folly in marrying Canaanites rather than in marrying two wives together, for which he is called profane, and sets out three counts of grief — that he married without his parents' consent, that he married where there was no religion, and that the wives themselves were provoking.
Clarke suspects a calculation beneath it, the wives being very likely daughters of Hittite chiefs by whom Esau meant to strengthen his secular power and influence; Wesley states the fault in a line.

Ellicott gets history out of the names, which show that the Hittites spoke a Semitic tongue, notes that the later genealogy of Esau lists the wives differently, and judges that these two verses would stand more rightly at the head of the following chapter.

sides.position: in marrying two wives together, for which perhaps he is called a fornicator
in marrying Canaanites, strangers to the blessing of Abraham and under the curse of Noah

themes: wives of the daughters of Heth
the names of the Hittite women

schools.summary: Gill makes the marriage itself the trouble, since it was contrary to their will that any of their children should marry Canaanites — and those the worst sort, the Hittites — Abraham having laid a strict injunction on his servant against it; he adds that the women were disagreeable both in religion, being idolaters, and in temper, being proud, haughty and disobedient, as all three Targums intimate.

Clarke draws the line the other way, that it was not the marriage but the persons, who by their perverse ways brought bitterness into the hearts of Isaac and Rebekah; he closes the chapter judging Isaac's denial of his wife much less excusable than Abraham's, since Abraham told no falsity but only suppressed a part of the truth.
Keil and Delitzsch let the verse stand as written, without comment.

debates.question: Was the bitterness caused by the marriage or by the women?

sides.position: the marriage itself, being with Canaanites against Abraham’s express injunction
not the marriage, improper as it was, but the persons and their perverse ways

themes: a grief of mind unto Isaac and Rebekah
